The test image shows a tomato stem split open longitudinally, revealing bleached/white internal tissue with dark structures (possibly sclerotia) embedded inside. The plant appears dead/collapsed.

Key features: stem, longitudinal cross-section, bleached interior, dark embedded structures, dried/collapsed tissue.

This strongly suggests Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot (stem sliced longitudinally showing sclerotia inside). Let me check reference images to confirm, starting with the top candidates.

This reference matches perfectly - same Bugwood series (5593844 vs test 5593851), same black plastic mulch background, same bleached stem with dark sclerotia visible on the surface. The test image is the split-open version of this same stem. Let me check one more reference from this class and one alternate candidate.

The second Sclerotinia reference is a perfect match - longitudinally split stem with large dark grayish-black sclerotia embedded in bleached white tissue, exactly like the test image. Now I need to check 6 more classes to fulfill the budget requirement.

I've now viewed 9 references from 8 different classes (2 from Sclerotinia). Summary of comparisons:

- **Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot/Bugwood_21**: Same Bugwood series as test image (5593844 vs 5593851), identical black plastic mulch background, bleached stem with dark surface sclerotia
- **Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot/Bugwood_4**: Exact match - longitudinally split bleached/white stem with large grayish-black sclerotia embedded in the pith tissue
- **Southern_Blight**: Split stem but no embedded sclerotia, different tissue appearance
- **Alternaria, Rhizopus**: Microscopic views, no match
- **Gray_Mold**: Surface brown lesion only, no match
- **Bacterial_Wilt**: Cross-sectional streaming test, no match
- **Phytophthora_Blight**: Dark collapsed stems, no match
- **Bacterial_Canker**: Green stem with brown vascular rot, no embedded sclerotia

The test image is definitively Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot. The bleached/hollow stem split longitudinally showing embedded dark grayish-black sclerotia (rice-grain sized) is the diagnostic hallmark of this disease, and the Bugwood image series numbers confirm they're from the same source.
